description_full: Armstrong World Industries, Inc., together with its subsidiaries, engages in the design, manufacture, and sale of ceiling and wall solutions in the Americas. It operates through Mineral Fiber and Architectural Specialties segments. The company offers mineral fiber, fiberglass, metal, wood, felt, architectural resin and glass, wood fiber, and glass-reinforced-gypsum; and ceiling component products, such as ceiling perimeters and trims, as well as grid products that support drywall ceiling systems. It also designs, produces, and sources specialty ceilings, walls, and other interior and exterior architectural applications primarily for use in commercial settings; and manufactures ceiling suspension system (grid) products. It serves commercial and residential construction markets, as well as renovation of existing buildings sectors. The company sells its products to resale distributors, ceiling system contractors, wholesalers, and retailers comprising large home centers. Armstrong World Industries, Inc. was founded in 1860 and is headquartered in Lancaster, Pennsylvania.

financial_summary: Armstrong World Industries Inc is a mid-cap industrials business with a $7.0B market cap on $1.6B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +10% over the past three years and -4% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 22% against a 9% cost of capital — a 13-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, with gross margins sitting at 36%.

The business throws off $246M in free cash flow — roughly 15 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.15× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.5× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage of 13× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield of 2.6% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 2.4× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 27% operating margin runs 18pp above the Industrials median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 2.39x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-1.1% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 548 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted lower, down 5% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 19% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 29% and a beta of 0.91, it moves roughly with the market.
About $56.8M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 41% in the 2020 crash, 40% in the 2022 bear market and 75% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $113 (margin of safety -47%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 19%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $79.49 to $165 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Industrials peers: EV/EBITDA 16.5 vs 12.9 and P/FCF 28.3 vs 21.8 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 42% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 3.5% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 5.7% (vs the 8% bar).
The 11 covering analysts target $200 on average, 20% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 22% clears the cost of capital of 9.5% by 13pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.45).
It runs a 36% gross margin and converts 15% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 9/9 and cash conversion of 1.15x.
ROE of 34% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.1x equity multiplier).
It spends 1.0% of revenue on R&D and 1.4% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 0.5x net debt to EBITDA ($112.7M of cash against $406.7M of debt), with interest covered 13.1x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 7.1, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 9.5% over 3 years, 11.6% over 5 years and -3.9% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 17%).
At current returns, reinvesting 4% of profits supports about 0.9% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 8.5% a year over five years.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (0.9x, 6.7% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 25, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own a modest 1.6%, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
It returns 2.6% a year to shareholders (1.9% in buybacks and 0.9% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 2.4% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
people: With about 4,100 employees, each generates about $395K of revenue, in line with the Industrials median, and revenue has fallen 4.0% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $60K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $1.2M (3x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (1/10, lower is better).
